articles.title: Iran’s president says ‘we will never forget’ Minab school attack
articles.body:
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has renewed criticism of the US and Israel over an attack on February 28, the first day of their joint war on Iran, which he says killed 168 children at a school in Minab.

“The US government and Israeli regime bear responsibility for Minab’s 168 murdered children,” said Pezeshkian in a post on X. “We will never forget. This atrocity exposes the hypocrisy of those who claim to defend human rights.”

In September, a UN fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe the US was behind a deadly strike on a primary school in Minab on February 28 and that the attack amounted to a war crime.

In June, US President Donald Trump said “nobody” purposefully attacked a school in Iran, citing an ongoing investigation.

No agony is greater than a father burying the child he should still hold in his arms. The US government and Israeli regime bear responsibility for Minab's 168 murdered children. We will never forget. This atrocity exposes the hypocrisy of those who claim to defend human rights.

articles.title: Iran denies responsibility for Kuwait drone strike that killed two Italians
articles.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the accusations baseless and the incident "suspicious" and offered to cooperate on a joint investigation
articles.body: Iran denied responsibility on Thursday for drone strikes on Kuwait that killed two Italian nationals, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling the accusations baseless and proposing a joint investigation with Rome and Kuwait City.Araghchi spoke by telephone with his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts, Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah and Antonio Tajani, and later wrote on X that the incident was "suspicious and looks like a preecooked recipe for war.""We stand ready to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the incident," he added.Tajani had earlier told the Italian Senate that several Iranian drones struck Kuwaiti military facilities at around 2 pm local time (12 pm CET), including an air defence radar centre where two Italian specialists employed by arms company Rheinmetall were working.Kuwait's Al-Sabah condemned the attack as "a heinous Iranian aggression" and offered condolences to Italy.Senior spokesperson for Iran's armed forces Abolfazl Shekarchi flatly denied any Iranian military operation in the region and accused the US and Israel of staging a false flag attack to destabilise the area.IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency went further, citing an unnamed security source who alleged that Ukraine had deployed a network of thousands of drones across the region, including in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. It provided no evidence.The Iran embassy in Rome separately issued a statement categorically rejecting any Iranian role and warning against attempts to widen the war.Gulf states condemn TehranSaudi Arabia called for an immediate halt to Iranian attacks and said it held Tehran responsible for the consequences of its actions. Bahrain asked the UN Security Council to hold Iran accountable and demanded compensation for the damage.Qatar warned that repeated strikes on Kuwait risked undermining diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions. The UAE, Syria and Jordan also condemned the attack.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for increased pressure on Tehran and said Gulf security was directly linked to Europe's security.Iran has repeatedly struck Arab Gulf states with drones and missiles since the start of the war, saying it has targeted military bases and US-linked facilities, with Kuwait and Bahrain among the most frequently targeted countries.Tehran has urged its neighbours not to allow their territory to be used for attacks against Iran.Iran's army confirmed a separate drone attack on Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base earlier in November.Tajani had informed the Italian parliament on 8 October of a decision to relocate most of its troops from Kuwait, with only around 10 military personnel remaining in the country at the time of the attack.

articles.title: Trump says US has ‘victory at hand’ in war on Iran, offers Tehran chance for deal
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump says Washington has “victory at hand” in its war on Iran and is giving Tehran an opportunity to reach an agreement that could prevent further loss of life.

Speaking during a Thanksgiving call with US military personnel from his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida, Trump suggested that the timing of victory remained his decision.

“It’s going to be whenever I want it to be, to be honest,” he said.

Trump also said his administration was still offering Iran an opening to negotiate.

“We’re trying to be nice. We’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I’m not sure if they are gonna take advantage of that,” he said.

“Some people question why. Are they crazy? Maybe they are.”

The remarks come amid continued uncertainty over efforts to reach an agreement to end the US-Israel war on Iran.

articles.title: Iran’s Araghchi sees opportunities for ‘peace diplomacy’ after war
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says an end to the US-Israel war on Iran could pave the way for renewed diplomacy, economic development and international cooperation.

“With the consolidation of the Iranian people’s victories against the enemies of this land and the end of the recent imposed war, peace diplomacy can undoubtedly open new horizons and valuable opportunities,” Araghchi said in a message marking Isfahan Day, according to the IRNA news agency.

Araghchi accused the US and Israel of targeting Iran’s industrial and defence infrastructure, as well as damaging historical monuments and cultural heritage sites during the two recent wars.

He also highlighted the potential for post-war economic recovery, saying tourism and cultural exchanges could stimulate economic growth, expand cross-border cooperation and strengthen international relations.

The foreign minister did not announce any new diplomatic initiative or timetable for ending the war.

“The incident is suspicious and looks like a pre-cooked recipe for war,” he said in a post on X, adding that Iran stands ready to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the incident.

Earlier, Araghchi said he expressed his condolences over the death of the two Italian nationals in a phone call with his Italian counterpart Antonio Tajani, categorically denying Iranian involvement in the attack.

articles.title: Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian unit files for bankruptcy amid soaring fuel costs linked to Iran war
articles.body:
Budget carrier Norse ⁠⁠Atlantic has said its ⁠⁠Norwegian operating unit will file for bankruptcy protection due to soaring fuel costs caused by the war in Iran.

Norse is the ⁠⁠second European airline to enter bankruptcy proceedings this year after Latvia’s AirBaltic.

The company said it had not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs, with the board deciding to file a bankruptcy petition on November 27 with the Agder District Court in Norway for its operating subsidiary.

“The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse ‌‌Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations,” Norse’s Chief Executive Eivind Roald said in a statement.

articles.title: Deadly attack on Saudi refinery raises tensions as fighting escalates in Yemen
articles.body:
An attack on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan oil refinery has killed a Nepali worker, injured several others and disrupted operations, as fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen’s Houthis intensifies.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said an aerial projectile struck the facility on Thursday, sparking a fire and forcing a temporary suspension of some operations.

The ministry did not identify who carried out the attack, but the Saudi-led coalition blamed the Houthis and warned that further strikes on civilian infrastructure would be met with a military response.

The coalition later claimed to have destroyed a Houthi missile launch platform in Yemen’s Hodeidah governorate.

Meanwhile, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces reported hundreds of strikes against Houthi positions, claiming to have killed or wounded scores of fighters.

The escalating violence is worsening Yemen’s humanitarian crisis, with the UN reporting more than 360,000 people displaced since August.

"There was never any coordination. The foreign minister said that they would talk to their allies in the future. articles.title: Georgia’s Planned Surrogacy Ban Draws Church Support and Opposition Criticism
articles.summary: Georgian Dream announced its plan on November 22
articles.body: Georgian Dream's plan to ban surrogacy has won the backing of the Georgian Orthodox Church, but opposition politicians say the move will take away the chance of having children from families who cannot conceive without medical assistance. The debate intensified this week after Catholicos-Patriarch Shio III publicly welcomed the proposal, describing it as an important step towards Georgia's spiritual and moral renewal. Opposition leaders Zurab Japaridze and Nika Gvaramia strongly disagreed, warning that the ban would leave more families childless and force people to seek treatment abroad. Georgian Dream announced its plan on November 22. Parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia said the party would introduce legislation to prohibit surrogacy completely, citing concerns about human trafficking, the exploitation of women, and children's rights. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze called the move a "principled decision." He argued that exploitation was an inherent part of surrogacy and could not be prevented through regulation. "Surrogacy is a very serious phenomenon, first and foremost in terms of the exploitation of women. No matter how you regulate it, exploitation remains exploitation. The exploitation of women is an essential element of surrogacy. Therefore, regulation does not solve the fundamental problem of surrogacy," Kobakhidze said. He acknowledged that the industry contributed to the economy but said ethical concerns had taken priority. Kobakhidze also confirmed that the government had consulted the Georgian Orthodox Church before announcing the plan. He said the Patriarchate had supported a ban. "We are in constant communication with the Patriarchate, and there is no problem in this regard. Of course, we also held consultations on surrogacy. Their position was that it would be better for surrogacy to be banned," he said. The following day, November 23, Patriarch Shio III voiced his support during a sermon at St. Nino's Monastery in Bodbe. "I would like to express my great satisfaction with the new initiative that we all heard about yesterday. It concerns the prohibition of surrogacy in Georgia. Dear brothers and sisters, this is a very important decision," he said. The Patriarch described surrogacy as a practice associated with serious sins and said banning it would contribute to the country's spiritual and moral renewal. He also confirmed that the Church and government had discussed the issue before the announcement. "I am very pleased that this decision of yours stems from your Christian worldview and reflects your concern for our Church and for strengthening and promoting Christian and traditional values in our country," Shio III said. Prime Minister Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili, President Mikheil Kavelashvili and other government officials attended the service at Bodbe. The Church has opposed surrogacy for years. In his 2014 Christmas Epistle, the late Patriarch Ilia II questioned whether a family raising a child born through surrogacy could truly be happy. Shio III's latest comments, however, are among the clearest public expressions of Church support for a government move to prohibit the practice. [caption id="attachment_118326" align="alignnone" width="886"] A surrogate and future parents. Source: americansurrogacy[/caption] Opposition warns of consequences for families Opposition politicians say a complete ban would punish people who already face serious difficulties having children. Nika Gvaramia, a leader of the Coalition for Change, called the proposal "shameful and cruel." He accused Georgian Dream of depriving thousands of women of the chance to become mothers because of health conditions that prevent them from giving birth. "A shameful and cruel decision! For the sake of 'making peace' with the Patriarchate, they are depriving thousands of women of the opportunity to become mothers! Women who are not unwilling to give birth, but are unable to do so because of health conditions!" Gvaramia wrote on social media. He also questioned the impact on families and Georgia's already difficult demographic situation, asking how many children would never be born as a result. Girchi - More Freedom leader Zurab Japaridze also criticized the plan. He argued that banning surrogacy would not remove demand but would push people to seek arrangements in other countries. "The consequences of banning surrogacy will be more families left childless, more Georgians forced to move abroad, and more tragedies," he wrote. He went on to question the religious justification for the decision, saying, "How can you take away a newly established family's opportunity to have a child and believe that this is what God wants?" he asked. Japaridze also questioned why the government considered surrogacy unacceptable while allowing the gambling industry to operate. Kobakhidze was asked about the comparison and argued that the two sectors were fundamentally different. He pointed out that casinos had been operating in Georgia for years and formed part of the country's tourism industry. He said imposing abrupt restrictions on gambling would cause serious economic problems. A growing fertility industry The proposed ban would affect an industry that has attracted international clients for years. Georgia became a more prominent destination after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 disrupted the Ukrainian surrogacy market, previously one of the main choices for foreign clients. A Deutsche Welle report published in October 2026 estimated that around 19 clinics in Georgia offer surrogacy services. Arrangements through agencies in Tbilisi and Batumi cost approximately €45,000 to €55,000, while surrogate mothers interviewed for the report said they typically received between €18,000 and €28,000. Research on the sector recorded 4,674 children born through surrogacy in Georgia between 2019 and 2024. Kirtskhalia has claimed that foreign nationals account for 98% of those using the services, although he did not provide supporting data. The industry has also faced criticism over the treatment of surrogate mothers and a lack of effective state oversight. In its 2025 report on Georgia, the Council of Europe's Group of Experts on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings (GRETA) noted that commercial surrogacy was legal but that no specific law or bylaw ensured state regulation of the practice. It said recruitment standards were largely left to individual clinics and urged the authorities to address the risk of trafficking. The report also referred to a February 2025 investigation into a possible trafficking case involving Thai women brought to Georgia as surrogate mothers. Investigators suspected that the women had been forced to undergo egg harvesting. Three were taken to a shelter for trafficking victims, while four foreign nationals were questioned. The investigation was ongoing at the time of the report. Other foreign surrogate mothers have reported poor living conditions, unpaid compensation and health problems after childbirth. In 2025, investigators recognized dozens of women as victims in cases involving suspected exploitation. These cases have raised questions about how the industry should be regulated and how women can be better protected. The government argues that a ban is the only way to address the exploitation, while critics say stronger oversight would be a better response than ending the practice altogether. What happens next? The proposed ban would apply to surrogacy arrangements involving both Georgian citizens and foreign nationals. Kirtskhalia has clarified that in vitro fertilization (IVF) would remain legal and regulated. This is not the first attempt to restrict the industry. In 2023, the government submitted a bill that would have banned surrogacy services for foreign nationals and moved the sector towards an altruistic model. The bill did not advance, and the existing legal framework remained in place. The latest proposal has not yet been formally submitted to Parliament. No draft legislation or timetable has been announced. It is therefore still unclear what would happen to existing contracts, ongoing pregnancies, embryos and families already receiving treatment if the ban goes ahead. For now, surrogacy remains legal in Georgia. Much will depend on the wording of the proposed legislation and how the government plans to put it into effect. A complete ban would bring a major change to an industry that has developed over many years and become an established part of the country's international fertility-treatment market. By Team GT

articles.summary: Civic groups participate in a rally marking the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination in Jongno District, Seoul, March 15
articles.body: Civic groups participate in a rally marking the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination in Jongno District, Seoul, March 15. Korea Times photo by Kang Ye-jin Migrant support groups expressed hope Friday that the Constitutional Court’s landmark ruling against a blanket ban on foreign residents’ political activities will give residents greater freedom to speak out on issues that directly affect their lives. In a 6-3 decision Thursday, the court found the Immigration Act provision unconstitutional, 49 years after it was introduced. The court said the ban violated the principle of proportionality by restricting foreign residents’ freedom of expression more than necessary. For years, the broad restriction on political activities has left foreign nationals uncertain about where the line falls between legitimate advocacy and prohibited activity, according to Udaya Rai, head of the Migrants' Trade Union. "Immigration authorities have interpreted the provision too broadly. We have long feared visa-related disadvantages because even speaking at a rally organized by a political party or taking part in a public forum could be interpreted as political activity," Rai said. For the Seoul Branch of the Native Language Teachers Union (KGLU NTU), the ruling affirms foreign residents' right to have a say in the policies that shape their everyday lives. "This ruling affirms our basic human and democratic rights to engage with the government, speak out about our living and working conditions and advocate for our rights without fear of reprisal," said the KGLU NTU chair, surnamed Day. "We believe this ruling provides clarity on how foreigners living in Korea can participate fully in society. This is a significant step forward for human rights, and we fully support it." Justices take their seats to deliver rulings at the Constitutional Court's courtroom in Seoul, Thursday. Yonhap Introduced in 1977, the provision broadly prohibited foreign nationals residing in Korea from engaging in political activities. A 2005 amendment added an exception for activities permitted under other laws, but it did little to narrow the scope of the ban. Although violations are not subject to criminal punishment, foreign residents can face administrative measures, including orders to leave the country. The case began in 2021, when two Mongolian students in Korea sought to learn about presidential candidates' policies toward foreign residents so they could urge them to address discrimination and provide broader protection for their basic rights. After learning of the ban, they filed a constitutional complaint on July 2, 2021, arguing that the restriction could discourage them from expressing their views. Five years and five months later, the court issued a ruling of constitutional nonconformity. It allowed the provision to remain in force until Dec. 31, 2028, giving lawmakers time to revise it. The decision does not give foreign nationals an unrestricted right to engage in political activities. Restrictions under separate laws, including bans on joining political parties and making political donations, remain in place. “The decision confirms that foreigners’ political expression is also protected under freedom of expression, which is a fundamental human right,” said Kim Kwang-jae, an attorney at Shin & Kim who represented the petitioners. Kim said the court took into account that the vague provision could discourage foreign residents from expressing even ordinary opinions or calling for better treatment. "The court recognized the chilling effect caused by unclear rules and the difficulty of seeking remedies as key grounds for its decision. This ruling could also serve as a standard for reviewing other regulations affecting foreigners in the future," he explained. The ruling is also likely to prompt scrutiny of current administrative practices that may discourage foreign residents from speaking out, including immigration authorities' requirements that some international students on scholarships pledge to refrain from political activities. Migrants stage a rally at Seoul Station on the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination in February 2024. Korea Times photo by Choi Joo-yeon "The ball is now in the National Assembly's court," said Kim Seon-taek, a professor of law at Korea University. "The Constitutional Court said that political activities threatening the national interest, security or public order can still be restricted. But what exactly counts as such activity? The law needs to spell that out." The professor said lawmakers should adopt a framework in which political activities are generally permitted, with specific exceptions clearly laid out. "The Assembly should consult migrant groups, legal experts and civic organizations when drawing up the revisions," he added. CEC BiH Certifies Candidate Lists for Election of Delegates to FBiH House of Peoples
articles.body: The Central Election Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina (CEC BiH) today certified the candidate lists for the election of delegates from cantonal assemblies to the House of Peoples of the Parliament of the Federation of BiH, specifically for the following cantons: Una-Sana, Central Bosnia, Herzegovina-Neretva, West Herzegovina, and Canton 10. The Assembly of the Una-Sana Canton submitted a total of 12 candidate lists to the CEC, containing 17 candidates for delegates to the House of Peoples of the Parliament of the Federation of BiH. Five candidate lists were submitted for the election of delegates from the Bosniak constituent people, containing nine candidates; two lists were submitted for the election of delegates from the Serb constituent people, containing two candidates; three lists were submitted for the election of delegates from the Croat constituent people, containing three candidates; and two lists were submitted for the election of delegates from the “Others” category, containing three candidates. The Central Election Commission of BiH certified ten candidate lists that met the requirements for certification for the House of Peoples of the Parliament of the Federation of BiH. The candidate list of the “Movement for a Modern and Active Krajina” ( Pokret za modernu i aktivnu Krajinu ) was rejected due to a discrepancy in the declaration of affiliation with constituent peoples between 2022 and 2026. Additionally, the submitter of the candidate list, Mehmed Mahmić, will be notified to submit a new declaration of acceptance of candidacy using the prescribed form. The Assembly of the Central Bosnia Canton submitted a total of 12 candidate lists, containing 22 candidates for delegates to the House of Peoples of the Parliament of the Federation of BiH. For the election of delegates from the Bosniak constituent people, five candidate lists containing ten candidates were submitted; for the election of delegates from the Serb constituent people, one candidate list containing one candidate was submitted; for the election of delegates from the Croat constituent people, five candidate lists containing ten candidates were submitted; and for the election of delegates from the “Others” category, one candidate list containing one candidate was submitted. The Central Election Commission of BiH certified 11 candidate lists that met the requirements for certification, while it rejected the candidate list of Armin Kukić due to a discrepancy in his declared affiliation in 2022. The Central Election Commission certified all candidate lists submitted from the Assembly of the Herzegovina-Neretva Canton, the Assembly of the West Herzegovina Canton, and the Assembly of Canton 10. The Assembly of the Herzegovina-Neretva Canton submitted a total of 14 candidate lists, containing 28 candidates for delegates to the House of Peoples of the Parliament of the Federation of BiH. For the election of delegates from the Bosniak constituent people, two candidate lists were submitted, containing seven candidates; for the election of delegates from the Serb constituent people, three candidate lists were submitted, containing three candidates; for the election of delegates from the Croat constituent people, seven candidate lists were submitted, containing 16 candidates; and for the election of delegates from the “Others” category, two candidate lists were submitted, containing two candidates. The Assembly of the West Herzegovina Canton submitted a total of five candidate lists, containing 17 candidates for delegates to the House of Peoples of the Parliament of the Federation of BiH. For the election of delegates from the Croat constituent people, five candidate lists were submitted, containing 17 candidates. The Assembly of Canton 10 submitted a total of nine candidate lists, containing 18 candidates for delegates to the House of Peoples of the Parliament of the Federation of BiH. For the election of delegates from the Bosniak constituent people, two candidate lists were submitted, containing two candidates; for the election of delegates from the Serb constituent people, three candidate lists were submitted, containing four candidates; and for the election of delegates from the Croat constituent people, four candidate lists were submitted, containing 12 candidates. CEC member Željko Bakalar, who chaired today’s session, noted that all candidate lists for the indirect elections—which had been submitted to the CEC BiH headquarters over the past two days—were certified during this session. “We are still expecting lists for the indirect elections from the Zenica-Doboj Canton and the Sarajevo Canton; these have not yet been received at the headquarters of the Central Election Commission (CEC) of BiH,” said Balakar. Today, the Central Election Commission of BiH certified 24 candidate lists for the election of delegates to the Council of Peoples of Republika Srpska, out of a total of 29 submitted by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. A total of 29 candidate lists were submitted, containing 70 candidates for delegates to the Council of Peoples of Republika Srpska. For the election of delegates from the Bosniak constituent people, seven lists were submitted containing 20 candidates; for the election of delegates from the Serb constituent people, ten lists were submitted containing 22 candidates; for the election of delegates from the Croat constituent people, eight lists were submitted containing 20 candidates; and for the election of delegates from the “Others” category, four lists were submitted containing eight candidates. The CEC of BiH certified 24 candidate lists that fully meet the requirements for certification. Five candidate lists were partially certified—containing deficiencies related to ethnic declarations and the status of individuals currently holding mandates in municipal or city assemblies—while specific candidates on these lists who failed to meet the certification requirements were rejected. Today, the Central Election Commission also issued decisions regarding resignations, the termination of mandates, and the allocation of replacement mandates within the House of Representatives of the FBiH Parliament, as well as within various city and municipal councils, Fena writes.

Kashagan operator NCOC cleared of asset transaction limits by court
articles.summary: The court overturned a bailiff’s order prohibiting the company from conducting transactions involving its assets, according to the Telegram channel OilGazKZ
articles.body: The Atyrau Regional Court has partially upheld an appeal filed by North Caspian Operating Company (NCOC), the operator of the Kashagan oil field. The court overturned a bailiff’s order prohibiting the company from conducting transactions involving its assets, according to the Telegram channel OilGazKZ . «The Atyrau Regional Court partially granted NCOC’s appeal, ruling that the bailiff’s order prohibiting the company from taking actions involving its assets as part of enforcement proceedings to collect a 2.36 trillion tenge fine was unlawful,» the statement reads. NCOC had challenged five separate orders issued by a bailiff in July as part of enforcement proceedings related to the collection of an environmental fine totaling 2.356 trillion tenge (about $5 billion). Specifically, the company sought to have the following measures declared unlawful: the initiation of enforcement proceedings; the seizure of its real estate and vehicles; and a prohibition on the debtor carrying out certain actions involving its assets. The enforcement proceedings barred NCOC from entering into transactions that could reduce its assets, including the sale, donation, transfer or write-off of property, as well as the assignment of claims. The regional court found that the bailiff’s order did not cite a specific legal basis for the prohibition, explain why the measure was necessary or clearly identify the parties subject to the restriction. The order was also sent to the PSA, the organization representing the state’s interests in the project, for information and implementation. However, the bailiff did not clarify the PSA’s procedural status or establish whether it had the authority to enforce the restrictions. The court therefore concluded that the order was neither lawful nor adequately substantiated and ruled that it should be set aside. The judicial panel noted, however, that the bailiff retains the right to reimpose enforcement measures, provided they comply with legal requirements. The court rejected the remainder of NCOC’s appeal, leaving in force the seizure of the company’s real estate and vehicles, along with the other restrictions imposed as part of the enforcement proceedings. In early September, OilGasKZ reported , citing a response from the Ministry of Justice to an inquiry from Interfax-Kazakhstan, that enforcement proceedings against NCOC had been suspended. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice has denied reports that the collection of a 2.3 trillion tenge environmental fine from NCOC in favor of the state has been terminated. «NCOC has currently appealed the actions of the state bailiff. Therefore, the Atyrau Region Specialized Inter-District Administrative Court has requested the enforcement proceedings,» the ministry said in a statement. The ministry noted that, under subparagraph 13 of Article 42 of Kazakhstan’s Law «On Enforcement Proceedings and the Status of Enforcement Agents,» enforcement proceedings are suspended while the relevant materials are before a court, until the court returns them. Therefore, efforts to collect the funds from NCOC on behalf of the state will continue in accordance with the procedure established by law.

Ukraine proposes Black Sea ceasefire for food exports
articles.body:
Ukraine has proposed a military ceasefire in the Black Sea that will allow its food exports to continue, its foreign minister has said.

The sea has become a key theatre of fighting over recent months, as Kyiv and Moscow have targeted each other's vessels to disrupt maritime trade and fuel exports.

Andrii Sybiha told the national broadcaster Suspilne the proposal had been passed on to Ukraine's international allies and was awaiting a response from Russia.

He said: "We are ready for a ​ceasefire.

"We are grateful to India, Turkey and Egypt, ​which are playing ⁠an active ⁠and important role in de-escalating tensions in ‌the Black Sea, as well as in mediation efforts."

Russia has ​proposed that Ukraine suspend attacks ​on the Russian oil sector ⁠as part of the agreement, but that would only be accepted as part of a wider energy ceasefire, Sybiha added.

articles.title: Trump says victory in the war will be "whenever I want it to be," trying to give Iran "a chance to be smart"
articles.body:
President Trump told reporters Thursday that the U.S. would achieve victory and the war with Iran will be over, "whenever I want it to be," but that he is giving the Islamic Republic "a chance to be smart."

"We have victory at hand and it's going to be … whenever I want it to be," the president said as he took questions at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida after speaking on the phone with U.S. troops for Thanksgiving.

"We're giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I'm not sure if they are going to take advantage of that," he said of the Iranian regime.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump called Iran's negotiators "professional tap dancers" and reiterated previous remarks suggesting he would give them until the new year to agree to a peace deal.

articles.title: Trump adds Ukraine to warning against expanding war - after joint NATO statement singled out Russia
articles.summary: Donald Trump appears to have unilaterally changed the wording of a joint statement he shared with NATO chief Mark Rutte
articles.body:
Donald Trump appears to have unilaterally changed the wording of a joint statement he shared with NATO chief Mark Rutte.

The statement was put out after they met on Wednesday in Florida. It contained this notable sentence:

We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible.

Hours later, Trump posted his own version on his Truth Social platform:

We also talked about, at length, the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War - and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the War, as rapidly as possible!

A NATO official told Politico the original statement was officially agreed, suggesting Trump unilaterally amended the statement.

The White House has not commented.

articles.body: MOSCOW, November 27. /TASS/. The proposed bill on introducing penalties for sharing information on the aftermath of drone attacks inside Russia should be left to experts to dissect for now, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters. "If such initiatives have indeed been put forward, experts perhaps should provide justification for them," he said, commenting on the move by a group of Russian senators to submit a bill to the lower house of parliament seeking to make disseminating information about attacks inside Russia illegal. "Arguments should be presented by experts and those submitting such bills, so it would be wrong to comment on this before parliamentary debates take place," the Kremlin spokesman added.

articles.title: AI assists in preparing for talks — Russian special presidential envoy
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence certainly helps prepare for negotiations
articles.body: MOSCOW, November 27. /TASS/. Artificial intelligence (AI) helps prepare for negotiations and can not only handle practical tasks, but also lay the groundwork for geopolitical breakthroughs, Russian Special Presidential Envoy for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries and Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev said at the AI Journey conference. "Artificial intelligence certainly helps prepare for negotiations. Moreover, you can even type in a prompt and say ‘Here is what an agreement, say a diplomatic one, might look like,’ and artificial intelligence will offer its own thoughts. Then you can ask ‘How can this agreement better reflect Russia’s stance, provide stronger arguments for Russia’s concerns and address them?’ Indeed, this is a very important tool," Dmitriev said. The special presidential envoy emphasized that Russian AI models can be used not only to solve practical tasks, but also to prepare geopolitical breakthroughs.

articles.summary: Kuwait summoned the Iranian ambassador on Friday and handed him a "note of protest" over Iranian attacks on the country
articles.body:
Kuwait summoned the Iranian ambassador on Friday and handed him a "note of protest" over Iranian attacks on the country, including a drone strike Thursday that killed two Italians and injured two other people, the Kuwaiti Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

Deputy Foreign Minister Hamad Sulaiman Al-Mashaan condemned the attacks on Kuwait, "which constitute a flagrant violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity and a grave breach of international law," the statement said.

Al-Mashaan held the Islamic Republic of Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences and stressed Kuwait's right to self-defense, the ministry said.

Iran has denied involvement in Thursday's drone attack in Kuwait.

articles.body:
The UN nuclear watchdog said on Thursday it was working with Russia and Ukraine to arrange a ⁠new local ceasefire at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, following another loss of offsite power.

Russian forces seized the Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe's largest with six reactors, ⁠in the first weeks ​of ⁠Moscow's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Each side has since routinely accused the ⁠other of military activity that jeopardises nuclear safety.

The ​plant ⁠generates no power, but ‌needs electricity to keep nuclear fuel cool in its reactors.

articles.summary: Ukraine's military intelligence agency said on Thursday that North ​Korea has temporarily halted some military cooperation with Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine's military intelligence agency said on Thursday that North ​Korea has temporarily halted some military cooperation with Russia, including deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles, following ‌diplomatic tensions between the allies.

Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency said North Korean foreign minister Choe Son Hui announced the temporary suspension of cooperation last month, in response to an assertion by one of Russia's deputy foreign ministers that the Kremlin would help to de-escalate tensions between ​Seoul and Pyongyang.

North Korea has supplied Russia with weapons since 2023, according to a Reuters investigation, and with troops ​since 2024, including soldiers who fought Ukrainian forces after their incursion into Russia's Kursk region.

articles.summary: Ukraine's military has said it carried out a drone attack on a key missile fuel production site in Russia's Tula region overnight
articles.body:
Ukraine's military has said it carried out a drone attack on a key missile fuel production site in Russia's Tula region overnight.

Kyiv's forces worked with the Chernaya Iskra rebel movement inside Russia to attack the Efremov Synthetic Rubber Plant, which plays a key role in producing fuel used to launch Iskander ballistic missiles, Ukraine's general staff of the armed forces said on Telegram.

"It is with these missiles that the Russian army strikes Ukrainian cities, energy and civilian facilities. So each strike on Efremov means less ballistics that can fly to Ukraine," the unit said.

The scale of the damage caused by the attack was still being clarified, it added.

Ukraine's defence ministry said it was the third strike on the plant, which it described as "the beginning of the missile chain", in 11 months.

A woman has been injured after a drone attack in St Petersburg, according to local authorities.

The attack is said to have targeted two districts of Russia's second-largest city and caused damage to an apartment building.

St Petersburg, located in northwestern Russia, has increasingly faced security concerns linked to the ongoing war in Ukraine. Ukraine has stepped up its use of long-range drones against targets inside Russia, often focusing on military, industrial and infrastructure sites.

articles.title: UN agency trying to broker localised ceasefire at nuclear plant after power failure yesterday
articles.body:
The UN's nuclear agency has said it is engaging with Russia and Ukraine on a possible new localised ceasefire at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant.

The plant's connection to its only remaining external offsite power line was lost early yesterday morning, reportedly due to military activity, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.

That means the site is currently relying on two emergency generators "for essential nuclear safety and security functions", the agency said.

It is the 28th time the plant has been left in this critical situation since the Russian invasion in February 2022.

Estimates suggest the plant has enough diesel to run its generators for at least 10 days.

Previous ceasefires have been implemented on a number of occasions during the war, including for a week in September.

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant - which is the largest in Europe - has been occupied by Russian soldiers since the early days of the war.

articles.title: Russia preparing 'new mass strike' against Ukraine, Zelenskyy again warns
articles.summary: Russia is planning a massive wave of attacks against Ukraine in the coming days, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has claimed
articles.body:
Russia is planning a massive wave of attacks against Ukraine in the coming days, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has claimed.

"Unfortunately, we ⁠have information about ‌a new mass strike being prepared ‌by the Russians," the Ukrainian president said in his ⁠daily evening address.

He urged Ukrainians to pay attention to ⁠the alarms of ⁠missile threats in the coming days.

This echoes a warning issued earlier today, saying in a social media post that intelligence provides "clear information on the priorities that Russia sets".

Zelenskyy also said Ukraine was preparing countermeasures "accordingly".

In the past, he has accurately predicted such coming attacks, citing Ukrainian intelligence.

For context: Russia has been launching waves of strikes towards Ukraine every night, with normal attacks comprising around 100 drones and a few ballistic missiles, while larger attacks comprise several hundred drones.

Ukrainian air defences have been struggling with recent waves due to a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles.

A chemical plant in the Stavropol ‌region in Russia has been damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike overnight, an official said.

The Nevinnomyssky Azot plant was hit by the large-scale drone attack, the region's governor Vladimir Vladimirov said.

Debris from downed drones has been found in the vicinity of the industrial and energy facilities, Vladimirov said.

editorialRejections.title: Moldovan energy minister says Vulcanesti–Chisinau line prevents nationwide blackout in Moldova, after Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
editorialRejections.summary: The line automatically absorbed disruptions in the regional electricity system, while consumers of Moldova experienced only minor fluctuations
editorialRejections.reason: Ukraine coverage requires an international news source
editorialRejections.body: Moldovan energy minister says Vulcanesti–Chisinau line prevents nationwide blackout in Moldova, after Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure The new Vulcanesti–Chisinau power line has prevented a possible nationwide blackout in Moldova, following Russian attacks on energy infrastructure in the Odesa region. The line automatically absorbed disruptions in the regional electricity system, while consumers of Moldova experienced only minor fluctuations. Energy Minister Dorin Junghietu made statements to this effect during the In Context programme on Moldova 1 TV channel. According to the minister, the attacks took place last Friday, at about 10:30 and the city of Odesa was left practically without electricity. Under these circumstances, the new electricity transmission infrastructure played an important role in maintaining the stability of the national system. “As you know, on that day, Odesa was practically left without electricity, and we felt that shock only as a fluctuation. The national electricity system managed to cope precisely because the Vulcanesti–Chisinau power line had been commissioned and automatically absorbed that potential shock,” Dorin Junghietu said. The minister emphasized that, without the new line, the consequences for Moldova could have been much more serious, with a high risk of a widespread interruption of electricity supplies. “If we had still been using the old Isaccea–Vulcanesti–Kuchurgan line, we would have experienced a power outage. (...) Under the old configuration, there was a very high probability that we would have faced some kind of blackout,” the official said. Dorin Junghietu noted that risks to Moldova’s energy security persist, which is why the government ruled to move from a state of emergency to an alert status in the energy sector, without abandoning rapid-response mechanisms. He also said that Moldova continued to operate within an electricity system integrated with Ukraine’s, and that security developments in the region may affect energy supplies. “We must have mechanisms for rapid intervention in various scenarios, as was the case throughout the current year. (...) Following the attacks that took place in Ukraine during the past week, the Ukrainians set their export capacity to zero. Therefore, they are no longer commercially exporting a single megawatt of electricity,” the minister specified. At present, Moldova is meeting its electricity needs through imports from the Romanian market, particularly during peak hours, to compensate for insufficient domestic production. The Vulcanesti–Chisinau power line, approximately 157 kilometers long and with a capacity of 400 kV, was inaugurated and energized on November 8, 2026. It enables electricity to be transmitted from Romania directly to the center of the country, without passing through the Kuchurgan energy hub. Two other major interconnections are in preparation: the Balti–Suceava line, for which a contract worth 17.5 million euros has been signed, and Straseni–Gutinas, a project estimated at 130 million dollars and financed by the United States, the completion of which is planned for 2032. Ukraine’s energy infrastructure continues to come under Russian attacks, while electricity generation and transmission capacities remain affected. According to an assessment published by the International Energy Agency on November 4, 2026, attacks during the previous winter damaged or destroyed 8.5 GW of electricity generation capacity, while power outages affecting the population reached nearly 12 hours a day in last February. The IEA warns that new attacks on power plants, electricity grids and gas infrastructure continue to pose a risk of energy shortages in next winter too. According to a joint assessment conducted by the government of Ukraine, the World Bank, the European Union, and the United Nations, published on February 23, 2026, total direct damages in Ukraine exceeded 195 billion dollars as of December 31, 2025, while the energy sector recorded an approximately 21-per cent increase in damaged or destroyed assets compared with the previous assessment. The energy sector’s reconstruction and recovery needs are estimated at almost 91 billion dollars. editorialRejections.title: November 27, 2026 - 17:45 Macron hits back at French presidential hopeful who called Ukraine war 'not ours'
editorialRejections.summary: Abandoning support for Ukraine could jeopardize France's security and that of all of Europe in the short or medium term
editorialRejections.reason: Ukraine coverage requires an international news source
editorialRejections.body: Abandoning support for Ukraine could jeopardize France's security and that of all of Europe in the short or medium term. The war has existential significance for Europeans, French President Emmanuel Macron said.On November 26, the French leader spoke at an extraordinary EU summit focused on the budget. He urged leaders not to create doubt and confusion over support for Ukraine. If we abandoned Ukraine, we would jeopardize our security in the short or medium term, the French president stressed. According to him, EU assistance is critical, especially if US support is scaled back. Ukrainians are fighting for their country's sovereignty, but they are also on the front line of European security. The Ukrainians' fight is also our fight. It is a fight for Europe's security, because Vladimir Putin's targets are the European Union and NATO, Macron explained. He added that Europe stands united behind Ukraine and urged leaders to avoid naivety and irresponsibility. As president of France, I can tell you that what is happening in Ukraine is a matter of security for all French people, he said. Macron also noted that France has not allocated the largest share of its budget to aid Ukraine. The day before, French presidential candidate and Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner questioned support for Ukraine. I don't understand why we're sending troops to Ukraine when it's not our war, he said. Riner also believes that aid to Ukraine comes at the expense of other funding areas. France's presidential election will take place in 2027. Notably, after a summit of European leaders in Dublin, Macron addressed the French people. He said that supporting Ukraine protects France and that Ukraine has a place in NATO. Later, people close to Macron accused the United States of pressuring Ukraine during negotiations. They also criticized French politicians, including Marine Le Pen, who called for cuts to aid to Kyiv. France also expressed support for Ukraine following attacks on Russian vessels near Libya and in the Baltic Sea. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot stressed that Ukrainians are defending themselves against daily attacks.

editorialRejections.body: Croatia's High Criminal Court has overturned a ruling ordering the extradition to Germany of Volodymyr Zhuravliov, a suspect in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, the Ukrainian law firm representing him said on Nov. 27. In August, Croatian authorities detained scuba diver Zhuravliov under a European arrest warrant issued by Germany in connection with the September 2022 explosions that damaged the pipelines built to funnel Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. German authorities accuse him of helping to place explosives on the pipelines as part of a covert operation conducted from a rented sailing yacht that departed from the port of Rostock. A Croatian court authorized Zhuravliov's extradition to Germany on Sept. 18, as he requested political asylum in Croatia. The law firm representing Zhuravliov said Croatia's High Criminal Court upheld an appeal filed by his attorneys on Nov. 23, overturning the extradition ruling and sending the case back for reconsideration. The appeals court found the lower court's decision premature and asked it to seek further clarification from German authorities on the two European arrest warrants, the charges, and the scope of the criminal proceedings. "(Zhuravliov's) extradition to Germany remains an open question," the Ukrainian law firm said on Facebook. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later. The Polish court argued that the Nord Stream sabotage could be considered a justifiable act in the context of Ukraine's defense against Russia. German investigators previously linked the sabotage to a pro-Ukraine group, allegedly led by another Ukrainian national, Serhii Kuznietsov , who is already in German custody after being detained in Italy in August 2025. The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics. Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.

editorialRejections.title: Moldova must build interceptor drones despite neutrality, PM says Moldova must build domestic interceptor drones and modernize its military despite constitutional neutrality, Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said on public broadcaster Moldova 1, as defense spending remains at 0.6% of GDP.
editorialRejections.summary: Speaking on the Bună seara talkshow, Tofan compared Moldova's military budget with European and Baltic benchmarks
editorialRejections.reason: Routine, incomplete or malformed headline outside the DNU brief
editorialRejections.body: Moldova must build domestic interceptor drones and modernize its military despite constitutional neutrality, Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said on public broadcaster Moldova 1, as defense spending remains at 0.6% of GDP. Speaking on the Bună seara talkshow, Tofan compared Moldova's military budget with European and Baltic benchmarks. He noted that Lithuania allocates 5.4% of GDP to defense—nearly 50 times Moldova's total defense spending in absolute terms. Despite tight fiscal constraints, Tofan said gradual investment in military equipment and training is unavoidable. “Defense accounts for 0.6% of our GDP. Donald Trump is telling Europeans they must spend 5%—it started at 2% and demands have grown,” said Tofan. “On the one hand, we must strengthen our defense and, with the limited resources we have, invest in our soldiers, equip them, and train them.” Beyond hardware procurement, Tofan said Moldova's primary guarantee of peace and security remains its close partnership with European allies. He also criticized parts of the domestic opposition, accusing them of spreading disinformation and fueling public fear. “Our main source of security and peace is our very close relationship with our European partners, who we know defend us and care about our security,” said Tofan. “I am deeply alarmed by some opposition figures who spread chaos everywhere and frighten people into believing we want to drag the country into war, because they do not want what is best for the country.” He added that those political actors benefit from public anxiety and instability. “Sometimes I get the impression they want to set this country on fire, but we will not let them do that,” said Tofan. Tofan said Moldova already has skilled engineers, electricians, and mechanical specialists working in the wiring harness industry, particularly in the north of the country. He argued that a new legal framework should harness this local workforce to manufacture interceptor drones domestically. The prime minister also rejected opposition claims that drones violating Moldovan airspace or crashing on Moldovan territory were Ukrainian, stating that recovered unmanned aerial vehicles shown to the public were Russian-made. “We should not be overly cautious or afraid of our own shadow, buying foreign drones instead of producing our own,” said Tofan. “We can no longer ignore reality. We can be a neutral state, yet one with a capable, self-respecting military that we must gradually strengthen.” Addressing bilateral ties with Moscow, Tofan said Chișinău wants peaceful relations and normal trade with Russia, but argued that the current Kremlin leadership seeks to restore its empire and undermine neighboring states. He added that Ukrainian military resistance currently shields Moldova's own freedom. “We want a peaceful relationship with Russia. Nothing would make us happier than for Russia to be a normal country to which we could export and with which we could maintain normal ties,” said Tofan. “Unfortunately, it is currently led by people who want to rebuild an empire, and this Kremlin administration's goal is to undermine surrounding countries. They have very detailed plans regarding Moldova.” Tofan's remarks follow a November 25 televised statement by President Maia Sandu, who said Moldova could begin producing interceptor drones in 2027 using technology transferred from Ukraine. That same evening, the Russian Embassy in Chișinău issued a statement alleging an unspecified “anti-Russian provocation” that it said would severely worsen bilateral relations, without providing evidence to support the claim. Political analyst Anatol Țăranu told Radio Moldova that Moscow's accusations are unfounded, noting that Chișinău has no interest in escalating tensions. “Chișinău has no interest in this, at least based on everything visible and publicly known,” said Țăranu. “The war in Ukraine has pushed Moldovan-Russian relations into crisis, and it is unclear why Chișinău would want to deepen that crisis.”

editorialRejections.body: US President Donald Trump altered the joint statement agreed with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte following their meeting in Florida. In a social media post, the American leader included Ukraine alongside Russia in a warning about the risk of the war escalating, while the original text referred only to Russia, IPN reports. In a joint statement issued on Thursday, the two said they had discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that could lead to the war spreading, whether intentionally or unintentionally, as well as the need to find a peaceful resolution to the conflict as quickly as possible. This version of the statement was published by both the White House and NATO. Against this backdrop, a NATO official told Politico on condition of anonymity that the original text was the statement formally agreed upon by the two leaders. Donald Trump subsequently made unilateral changes to the version posted on social media. Meanwhile, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul warned Ukraine against expanding the geographical scope of its war with Russia after Kyiv attacked Russian vessels in the Mediterranean, in the Libyan port of Benghazi, and in the Baltic Sea. Germany’s top diplomat reaffirmed Ukraine’s right to self-defence but urged Kyiv to avoid escalating the conflict or posing any risks to shipping and security in the Baltic Sea region. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni also stressed that Ukraine has the right to defend itself, while emphasizing the need to safeguard Europe’s borders and its citizens. For their part, the Libyan authorities lodged a formal complaint with the UN General Assembly and Security Council, calling for an international investigation into Ukrainian attacks on Russian ships in the port of Benghazi.

editorialRejections.title: November 27 Trump adds Ukraine to warning against expanding war, diverging from joint NATO statement
editorialRejections.reason: Editor rejected this or a closely matching story
editorialRejections.body: U.S. President Donald Trump departed from a published joint statement with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Nov. 26, adding Ukraine to a warning against expanding the war that was originally directed solely at Russia. The change comes amid growing concerns among European allies over the geographical expansion of Russia's war against Ukraine, following recent Russian airspace violations in Poland and a Ukrainian strike on a Russian warship in the Mediterranean Sea. Trump and Rutte met at the U.S. president's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Nov. 25, with Russia's war against Ukraine and the conflict in Iran among the primary topics of discussion. In the joint statement released following the meeting, the two leaders emphasized "the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war." Hours later, Trump published his own version of the statement on Truth Social , referring to "the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War." A NATO official speaking on condition of anonymity told Politico that both sides had agreed to the original statement, indicating that Trump had subsequently changed the wording unilaterally. The White House did not respond to Politico's request for comment. In a separate social media post on Nov. 26, Trump said he had urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end military aggression across Europe during their meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Trump also expressed optimism about the possibility of reaching a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The revised wording comes as European leaders grapple with the risk of the war spreading beyond Ukraine's borders. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul separately warned against the geographical expansion of the war on Nov. 26, while reaffirming their countries' support for Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Nov. 23 that Ukrainian forces had sunk the Russian corvette Merkury in the Mediterranean Sea off the coast of Benghazi, Libya. Meanwhile, a series of Russian airspace violations in Poland has heightened security concerns among NATO allies, with Warsaw raising the possibility of NATO intercepting Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory.

editorialRejections.title: November 26, 2026 - 23:35 Black Sea tensions risk dragging US and NATO into Russia's war against Ukraine - CBS News
editorialRejections.summary: The number of incidents in the Black Sea has increased nearly tenfold in 2026
editorialRejections.reason: Editor rejected this or a closely matching story
editorialRejections.body: The number of incidents in the Black Sea has increased nearly tenfold in 2026. Rising tensions in the region have reached NATO's borders, creating a direct risk of drawing the Alliance and the United States into the war, CBS News reports.According to NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell, fewer than 50 incidents were recorded in the Black Sea in 2025, while this year the number has reached between 400 and 500. As a result, the Black Sea has become even more dangerous for seafarers than the Strait of Hormuz amid the confrontation between the United States and Iran. Since the beginning of the year, at least 40 crew members have been killed in the Black Sea, compared with 25 in the Strait of Hormuz. O'Donnell emphasized that the region is critical to global trade, particularly grain and fuel supplies, and that any disruption to food and energy flows would have global consequences, affecting the United States as well. Meanwhile, NATO's Black Sea member states — Romania, Bulgaria, and Türkiye — are finding it increasingly difficult to monitor their maritime borders. According to Romanian Navy Captain Mihai Iordache, the Romanian fleet is operating at the limits of its capacity, constantly neutralizing explosive hazards using divers and underwater drones. Four years ago, we were ready for one drifting mine, and right now we are ready for tens of drifting drones. We don't have enough people, personnel, or equipment to deal with all the commercial ships and all the drones that we have, Iordache said. Amid growing threats on NATO's eastern flank, including the recent crash of Russian cruise missiles in southeastern Poland and repeated drone incursions into the Alliance's airspace, NATO officials in Brussels reaffirmed their readiness to defend allies under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. I would say that there should be no doubt about NATO's willingness and ability to act, NATO spokesperson Martin O'Donnell emphasized. Maritime security and establishing a ceasefire in the Black Sea remain among the most challenging issues in the negotiation process. Kyiv previously stated that Ukraine expects pressure from several countries that directly depend on maritime supplies to encourage Russia to agree to a ceasefire in the Black Sea. Meanwhile, as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan explained, Russia refuses to agree to a separate ceasefire in the Black Sea without signing a comprehensive, long-term peace agreement with Ukraine, while the negotiation process itself remains effectively deadlocked over the territorial issue of Donbas.

editorialRejections.title: How Kazakhstan will build a uranium reserve worth 7 years of Kazatomprom output
editorialRejections.summary: President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has ordered the creation of a strategic uranium reserve to meet the long-term needs of Kazakhstan’s nuclear industry
editorialRejections.reason: Explainer headlines are excluded
editorialRejections.body: President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has ordered the creation of a strategic uranium reserve to meet the long-term needs of Kazakhstan’s nuclear industry. Mining companies will supply uranium for the state reserve under special contracts, the Agency for Atomic Energy (AAE) told Kursiv.media . However, the planned reserve will extend beyond physically stockpiled uranium to cover the entire nuclear fuel supply chain. «The reserve is not limited to physically stockpiled uranium. Rather, it is structured across the entire supply chain, from resources still in the ground to finished nuclear fuel. Specifically, in the long term, a portion of the uranium will remain underground. In parallel, the plan includes maintaining physical stocks of natural uranium and securing contractual supply commitments. The availability of low-enriched uranium and finished nuclear fuel is also factored in to meet short-term needs,» the agency said in response to Kursiv . media’s inquiry. The goal of this multilevel approach is to ensure a stable, long-term supply of raw materials and nuclear fuel for Kazakhstan’s future nuclear power plants (NPPs). The specific format and arrangements for establishing the strategic reserve have yet to be finalized. As a result, the agency is not currently providing details on pricing, funding sources or potential uranium supply commitments. Uranium producers currently sell their output at international market prices under either spot-market or long-term contracts. Domestic supplies, however, could be priced lower because of reduced transportation and other associated costs. According to the AAE, Kazakhstan plans to reserve 100,000 tons of uranium by 2040 and 150,000 tons by 2050 to meet the needs of its future nuclear power plants. Under existing uranium production contracts, subsoil users are required to keep their annual output within a range of plus or minus 20% of their contractual production obligations. Exceeding this threshold constitutes a breach of contract and could result in the agreement being terminated. Since uranium producers already have long-term and short-term supply contracts with buyers, additional arrangements could be introduced for new deposits, through extensions of existing contracts or by amending current agreements. A reserve of 150,000 tons would represent a substantial volume, equivalent to approximately seven years of production by Kazakhstan’s national uranium producer, Kazatomprom.
